implementation_notes: Ruby's idiomatic bulkhead is a bounded pool of resources, above all database and Redis connections: ConnectionPool.new(size: 8, timeout: 1) { create_conn } wraps each dependency, #with checks a resource out and returns it after the block, and once every slot is busy the next checkout waits up to the timeout and raises Timeout as the saturation signal. The classic thread-pool structure is replaced by checkout/checkin of a fixed-size pool; the same gem works for any expensive resource, and the sibling Concurrent::Semaphore form covers work that is not a pooled resource.

variants.name: connection_pool gem: bounded checkout per dependency
variants.implementation_notes: Ruby's idiomatic bulkhead is a bounded pool of resources, above all database and Redis connections: ConnectionPool.new(size: 8, timeout: 1) { create_conn } wraps each dependency, #with checks a resource out and returns it after the block, and once every slot is busy the next checkout waits up to the timeout and raises Timeout as the saturation signal. The classic thread-pool structure is replaced by checkout/checkin of a fixed-size pool; the same gem works for any expensive resource, and the sibling Concurrent::Semaphore form covers work that is not a pooled resource.
pitfalls: Pool size multiplied by processes and threads must stay inside the server's connection limit; forking servers duplicate pools per worker unless after_fork is handled.
The default timeout may be too long, so saturation appears as slow requests instead of a fast failure; map Timeout to a controlled response.
Nested checkouts (holding one pooled connection while acquiring another) deadlock the pool when all slots are held.
A resource returned dirty after a raise stays broken for the next borrower; reset or discard it in the block.

variants.name: Concurrent::Semaphore (or Concurrent::FixedThreadPool)
variants.implementation_notes: For work that is not a pooled resource, concurrent-ruby supplies the primitives: Concurrent::Semaphore#try_acquire and #release bound concurrent operations (try_acquire returns false immediately, acquire(timeout) waits), and Concurrent::FixedThreadPool runs tasks on a bounded worker set with its own queue. Choose the semaphore when the caller's thread should do the work and only admission must be bounded, the fixed pool when the work must not run on the caller; the framework replaces hand-written Mutex/ConditionVariable bookkeeping, not the pattern.
variants.code_sketch:
require "concurrent"

DB_SLOTS = Concurrent::Semaphore.new(8)

def query(sql)
  raise Busy, "db bulkhead saturated" unless DB_SLOTS.try_acquire
  begin
    db_call(sql)
  ensure
    DB_SLOTS.release
  end
end
pitfalls: The GVL means a semaphore bounds CPU-bound Ruby work but does not isolate it: native extensions that release the GVL still contend for the same cores.
try_acquire returns false immediately while acquire(timeout) waits and then continues - pick one deliberately and handle both paths.
ensure is mandatory: an exception between acquire and release permanently leaks a permit.
Ruby threads are OS threads, so a fixed thread pool per dependency multiplies threads; MRI cannot parallelise Ruby-level CPU work beyond the GVL.
Pool size multiplied by processes and threads must stay inside the server's connection limit; forking servers duplicate pools per worker unless after_fork is handled.
The default timeout may be too long, so saturation appears as slow requests instead of a fast failure; map Timeout to a controlled response.
Nested checkouts (holding one pooled connection while acquiring another) deadlock the pool when all slots are held.
A resource returned dirty after a raise stays broken for the next borrower; reset or discard it in the block.
